author: y3owk1n
body:
Three assertions named the admin surface by hand — `OPERATIONS = 39` in `packages/core/src/http/openapi.test.ts`, used twice, and `toHaveLength(28)` in `packages/core/src/auth/auth.test.ts`. Every ticket that added a route bumped all three, across two files; #171, #172 and #173 each did. ADR-0049 already ruled on that tax for migration counts.

## What changed for a reader of this repository

**Adding a route now edits no count anywhere.**

Each count is asked of a source the assertion is *not* already reading — the half of ADR-0049 that is easy to skip, because a count derived from the side under test agrees with itself, and an empty scan would then satisfy an empty expectation.

| Assertion | Held to |
| --- | --- |
| the two description scans in `openapi.test.ts` | **Hono's route table**, via `servedOperationCount` |
| the no-session sweep in `auth.test.ts`, which walks the *runtime* description | **`packages/core/openapi.json`**, the checked-in artifact, read off disk |
| the gated-route count | the description's admin operations minus the three session routes, **named** |

The third is the one worth looking at: the count was documented as "every admin route but the three that manage the session", so it is now that set difference rather than `26`. A fourth ungated admin route fails it, where the number would have been nudged to 27 by whoever added one.

Both emptiness guards are kept — two empty lists are equal, so each derivation asserts it found something before it is believed.

## Watched failing

Per the discipline ADR-0049 asks for, each derivation was made to fail and then restored:

- an operation deleted from the checked-in artifact → auth's sweep, `expected […28] to have a length of 27 but got 28`
- a route dropped from the router table → `expected […39] to have a length of 38 but got 39`
- `get /admin/store` wrongly added to the excused list → `expected [Array(26)] to deeply equal [Array(25)]`

## The ADR question the ticket asks to decide

**No second record.** ADR-0049 did not decide something about migrations that happens to generalise — every clause of it reached these counts unchanged, and a new ADR restating them for routes would leave the next surface that grows a count with two records to reconcile. It gains an **Applied again** section, and `docs/agents/writing-tests.md` carries the rule beside the migration one.

## Checks

`devbox run format`, `lint`, `typecheck` clean; the two touched files green (72 tests). The full gate is CI's — no generated artifact was touched.

Closes #188

author: prrthiksh
body:
## Summary

Restores the `SurfaceMountingManager` defensive guards that shipped on the 0.78.3 fork
([zeptonow/react-native#17](https://github.com/zeptonow/react-native/pull/17)) but were lost in the
0.85.3 port. The file was renamed `SurfaceMountingManager.java` → `.kt` between the two RN versions,
which broke patch matching. Five other renamed files from that PR (`MountingManager`,
`NativeAnimatedModule`, `NativeAnimatedNodesManager`, `NetworkingModule`, `ReactViewGroup`) were
re-derived by hand; this one was not — it carried only defensive guards, so nothing failed at build
or smoke-test time when it went missing. It surfaced as crashes in the field instead.

## Crashes this fixes

Both observed on Android build 26.8.5 (739):

1. `RetryableMountingLayerException: Unable to find viewState for tag 1572. Surface stopped: false`
   at `addViewAt`. Despite the name, this is **not** retried on the `IntBufferBatchMountItem` path —
   `MountItemDispatcher` only retries `DispatchCommandMountItem` — so it propagates and kills the app.
2. `IllegalStateException: Cannot remove child at index 3 from parent ViewGroup [...], only 3
   children in parent` at `removeViewAt`, wrapping an NPE thrown out of a third-party ViewManager
   (`react-native-maps`). The wrapping message is itself misleading: `childCount` is read *after* the
   partial removal, so the index was never actually out of range.

## Changes

All nine throwing `getViewState(...)` call sites become `getNullableViewState(...) ?: return`:

`addViewAt` (parent + child), `updateProps`, `updateLayout`, `updatePadding`, `updateOverflowInset`,
`updateState`, `sendAccessibilityEvent`, `setJSResponder`.

Three throws on the mount path become `return`:

- `removeViewAt` — non-ViewGroup parent
- `removeViewAt` — the `catch (RuntimeException)` rethrow around `viewGroupManager.removeViewAt(...)`
- `addViewAt` — the `IllegalStateException` / `IndexOutOfBoundsException` rethrows around
  `getViewGroupManager(...).addView(...)`

The now-unused `private fun getViewState` is deleted. This is required, not cosmetic: CI runs
`-PenableWarningsAsErrors=true` (`.github/actions/build-android/action.yml:69`) and an unused private
function is a Kotlin warning. Upstream `main` deleted it too, once all its callers were guarded.

## Deliberately unchanged

- `receiveCommand` and `getView` keep throwing `RetryableMountingLayerException`. Those take the
  `DispatchCommandMountItem` path, where the retry actually works. Upstream `main` still throws there.
- `addViewAt` keeps its two specific catch types rather than widening to `RuntimeException`, matching
  upstream and #17. Note the resulting asymmetry: an NPE out of a ViewManager's `addView` is still
  uncaught, while the same on `removeViewAt` is caught.

## Relationship to upstream

Upstream has since written equivalent guards — [#56389](https://github.com/facebook/react-native/pull/56389)
(`addViewAt`), [#57283](https://github.com/facebook/react-native/pull/57283), [#57181](https://github.com/facebook/react-native/pull/57181),
[#56762](https://github.com/facebook/react-native/pull/56762) — all present in `0.86-stable` and `main`,
**none backported to `0.85-stable`**. Upstream logs a soft exception where this PR returns silently;
we match #17 instead, to keep the change minimal. The `removeViewAt` catch-block rethrow has **no**
upstream equivalent — `main` still rethrows there as of 0.86.

This should drop out on the 0.86 upgrade, except for the `removeViewAt` catch block.

## Test Plan

- [ ] `./gradlew :packages:react-native:ReactAndroid:compileReleaseKotlin -PenableWarningsAsErrors=true`
- [ ] Build the AAR and smoke-test the app against it
- [ ] Order-tracking map: scroll the map cell out of view and back, background/foreground, navigate away

> Guards are silent by design (matching #17), so there is no signal when one fires. If we later want
> visibility, one `FLog.e` per site is logcat-only with no external routing.

author: xbmlz
body:
Phase 3 of the issue #51 refactor: §15 (diagnostics / validation policy) and §16 (observable deferred failures).

## The problem

A read that hits a truncated file kept whatever it had parsed and stopped there, silently. That is what most DICOM tooling does, but a caller cannot tell a complete file from a damaged one, and the package had no way to be strict.

Separately, `Dataset.Get` masks a failed deferred load as a plain "absent". A tag whose source file has gone away stayed listed by `SortedTags` and `Elements` while every read of it returned nothing.

## The API

Issue #51 proposed a `Strict`/`Warn`/`Tolerant` policy enum. This uses one hook instead, because `Diagnostic` implements `error`:

```go
// tolerant, but visible
OnDiagnostic: func(d godicom.Diagnostic) error { log.Printf("%s", d); return nil }

// strict -- the anomaly itself is the error
OnDiagnostic: func(d godicom.Diagnostic) error { return d }
```

One field, no enum, no second read path. Diagnostics are also logged at warn level, so an existing `Logger` sees them with no code change. `Diagnostic` carries the kind, tag, VR, byte offset, enclosing sequence path, and the `Need`/`Have` byte counts, and unwraps to the underlying cause.

## Coverage

All three parsers are wired — the in-memory reader, the streaming reader behind `ReadFile`/`Read`, and the shared byte parser behind sequence contents and `DecodeDataset` — plus the deflated hand-off, which would otherwise drop the hook.

Two things needed care:

- The streaming reader copies a defined-length sequence out to its own buffer and parses that from offset 0, so a diagnostic from inside one would have named the wrong byte. `readContext` now carries a base offset; `TestTruncationInsideSequence_OffsetIsFileRelative` asserts both readers name the same byte for the same damage.
- `readSequenceItems` and `readDefinedLengthSequence` return no error, so a hook error raised inside a sequence is latched on `readContext` and unwound by the enclosing loops. `TestReadBytes_HookErrorInsideSequenceFailsTheRead` also asserts exactly one diagnostic is reported, i.e. no double-reporting on the way out.

13 new tests (`diagnostic_test.go`), covering both readers, both modes, the sequence path, the offset equivalence, the deferred-load failure (`errors.Is(d, os.ErrNotExist)`), the exact error string, and that no hook keeps the pre-existing tolerant behaviour.

Local: `go build`, `go vet`, `staticcheck -checks=all`, `gofmt` all clean; full suite 780 passing.

author: varun29ankus
body:
`train`'s own documentation already asks for "a representative sample (10x-50x `num_clusters`)". Nothing enforced or even reported it.

`kmeans` clamps `k` to the number of points available, so requesting 1024 clusters and supplying 100 vectors produced **100 single-point clusters**: every centroid sitting exactly on a training vector, every residual collapsing towards zero, and the PQ codebooks trained on that degenerate residual set. The index reported success, returned poor results, and left behind a config that looked deliberate. No error, no warning.

Silence was the defect, so this fixes the silence. `warn_if_undertrained` logs when the ratio falls below 10 points per centroid — the lower bound of the documented guidance, and where FAISS draws the same line (it warns below 39 and refuses below 10).

## Deliberately not a clamp

I tried the clamp first. Three integration tests caught it, correctly:

- `train_fewer_vectors_than_clusters` and `config_persists_correctly` depend on `train` supporting fewer training vectors than clusters and recording the reduced count.
- `retrain_restores_cluster_count_and_clears_data` retrains with 20 vectors and legitimately expects 4 clusters. A 10x ratio would have silently reduced that to 2 — replacing one silent degradation with another.

So the cluster count is untouched. Rejecting undertrained configurations outright changes public behaviour that callers rely on, and that deserves its own deliberate change rather than riding along here.

## Also

`train`'s doc comment now states what ignoring the ratio costs. It previously gave the number as bare advice with no indication of the consequence, which is why the guidance was easy to ignore — including by our own test fixtures.

## Verification

`cargo fmt --check`; clippy with `--features logging` (where the `warn!` actually compiles), `--all-features --all-targets`, `--no-default-features`, and wasm32 `no_std`; `cargo test --all --all-features` — 48 test binaries, zero failures, including the three tests that rejected the clamp.

body:
Follow-up to autonomous-testing/api#904 (autonomous-testing/backlog#4252).

## Why

That PR makes the api commit `wopee/features/all/tests.json` **pretty-printed**, so a test-case edit renders as a reviewable diff in a GitHub PR. `fetchArtifact` in `src/tools/shared/handlers.ts` hands that file **straight into the model's context** with no truncation, so the added whitespace is pure token cost — and `fetch_project_summary` pulls the USER_STORIES artifact for *every* suite in a project, multiplying it.

The indentation is for humans reading a diff. The model gains nothing from it.

## What

`_compactArtifactContentForModel(type, content)` re-serializes USER_STORIES content compact at the tool boundary. File bytes in the project repo are untouched — this is context only.

- **Type-gated**: `APP_CONTEXT` / `GENERAL_USER_STORIES` are markdown and `PLAYWRIGHT_CODE` is TypeScript, where collapsing whitespace would corrupt the file.
- **Fails open**: content that doesn't parse is returned untouched — a broken artifact is still worth showing the model, which can say so.
- Structural whitespace only; escaped newlines inside `description` values survive (covered by a test).

The pure string transform lives in `src/tools/shared/artifactContent.ts` rather than `helpers.ts` because `node --test` runs in strip-only TS mode and cannot load the enum-bearing `types.ts` — that's why only pure-logic modules have tests in this repo today. The enum-typed gate stays in `helpers.ts`.

## Summary

Versioned snippets in the Sphinx docs (the Conan install examples and the FetchContent tag hint) hardcoded the release version, so they went stale on every bump. They now reference `|release|`, which `conf.py` derives from `cmake/version.cmake` — making a version bump a single-file change again.

Uses [sphinx-substitution-extensions](https://pypi.org/project/sphinx-substitution-extensions/) (new pinned entry in `doc/sphinx/requirements.txt`), which makes the standard `|release|` substitution work inside literal blocks:

- `conf.py` defines `|release|` in `rst_prolog` from the version it already parses out of `cmake/version.cmake`.

The pin `>=2024.2,<2026` resolves to 2025.2.19, the newest version compatible with the existing `sphinx>=7.4,<8` constraint.

A reference implementation of the Week 6-7 SQLi login-bypass `Challenge` (Vulnerability Set 1), adapted to match the real `breachbox.challenges.base.Challenge` interface already in `main` — hashed flag comparison, `VALID_CATEGORIES`/`VALID_DIFFICULTIES` metadata, discoverable via `discover_challenges()`.

What This PR Fixes

Pytest Warning Fix

  • Fixed PytestUnknownMarkWarning warnings caused by tests using @pytest.mark.timeout

timeout: Set test timeout in seconds

## Summary

- extend block templates with private local keys, registry-declared node references, readable names, and two-pass atomic relationship materialization
- add Button v6 Disclosure configuration, read-only effective semantics, Inspector diagnostics and repair, and the state-powered Disclosure block
- preserve existing persisted project schema and public `block.insert` result contracts
- add responsive Editor and scoped hydration remediation, performance coverage, regression tests, and synchronized implementation documentation

## Why

Connected blocks need to create ordinary editable components, block-owned Boolean State, and safe internal relationships in one insertion without persisting compiler metadata or introducing a second runtime model. Disclosure is the first and only production adopter.

## User and developer impact

Authors can insert a working Disclosure whose trigger, controlled content, and Boolean State remain editable through existing Layers and Inspector flows. Insertions are atomic, Undo/Redo remains one operation, duplicated roots receive independent internal state, and invalid relationships omit potentially false `aria-expanded` semantics while remaining repairable.

body:
## Context
A monitoring probe is being migrated from `role='client'` to `role='monitoring'` in production (held pending this PR). This exposed every place that tested `role != 'client'` as a proxy for "is staff" — that stopped being equivalent the moment a service account could hold a non-client role. `apps/backend-rag/backend/app/utils/service_accounts.py` (already on main) defines the real predicate, `is_human_team_member()`.

## Defect 1 — the live roster leaked service accounts; the existing cure targeted a dead router
`GET /api/team/members` is served by `team.py::get_team_members`, which did **no** role filtering. A separate `team_members.py` had already been patched correctly, but was **never registered** (`router_manifest.py` lists it disabled, both `router_registration.py` `include_router` sites commented out) — a "fixed" dead copy is exactly how the next reader concludes the problem is handled.

- Deleted `team_members.py` and its test outright rather than leaving a misleading disabled copy.
- Fixed all three query branches of the live `get_team_members` (visibility-rules, board/founders/management, department-default).
- Frontend: `useTeamMembers.ts`'s filtered `useTeamMemberOptions()` now excludes service roles too, for its other consumers — **but `hr/employees/page.tsx` does not consume that hook**, it reads the raw unfiltered `useTeamMembers()` and maps it straight into the Add-Employee "Team Member" select. Only the backend fix at `team.py` closes that specific page; it now also applies its own local filter (`isNonHumanRole`) as defense-in-depth. Added `htmlFor`/`id` linking that field's label to its `<select>` so its accessible-name test can locate the control (a pre-existing a11y gap, unrelated to the security fix, that blocked the new test from running at all).

## Defect 2 — "not a client" used as a proxy for "is staff" at four live authority gates
Routed through `is_human_team_member`: `deps/auth.py::require_team_member`, `crm_portal_integration.py::require_team_auth` (8 endpoints), `portal_invite.py` (invite send/history/resend — mints tokens, sends live email), `agentic_rag.py` (A/B experiment control + exposure view — preserving the exposure view's "or viewing own history" carve-out exactly). `debug.py` consumes `require_team_member` too and is fixed for free; it also carries its own admin check, so it was independently safe — this removes a latent inconsistency, not an open door.

## Defect 3 — found during this work, not in the original brief
`auth.py`'s PANOPTICON auto-clockin had two layers: the callee `_auto_clockin_if_needed` already checked `is_human_team_member` first and returned before any write; only the caller-side `spawn()` gate still read `role != "client"`. **Correcting the record explicitly**: this was NOT a data-integrity hole — the callee already caught it. It was a redundant, less-correct caller gate that spawned and immediately discarded ~288 pointless coroutines a day for a 5-minute probe. Fixed for consistency, not to prevent corruption that was never possible. Added the test coverage that was missing for this exact call site — nothing previously tested the `spawn()` decision itself, only the callee in isolation.

## General-form test
`test_router_manifest.py` gained a hash-pinned registry of every file listed as a disabled/dead router. Any content change to a pinned file fails loudly, forcing an explicit choice instead of a silent "fixed and forgotten" edit; any newly-disabled router that isn't pinned yet also fails. Forward-looking by design — this specific instance was closed by deletion, not caught retroactively by this mechanism.

## Testing
Every guilt test uses realistic free-text job titles from this column ("Tax Care", "Tax Lead") rather than "admin", which would prove nothing about this system's actual role values. Every changed guard mutation-verified: revert the cure, confirm red, restore, confirm green. Backend 126/126 passing, frontend 6/6 passing.

## Provenance
This patch was substantially authored by an earlier agent lane whose worktree died mid-task — a fork-dispatch failure unrelated to this repo (`fork failed: Device not configured`) left 385 uncommitted lines with nobody to verify them. Salvaged from `.worktrees/ops-fix-dead-roster-cure`, reviewed hunk by hunk (each of the 4 gates confirmed deny-service/allow-human; the frontend-doesn't-close-the-page finding above; the DEFECT-3 consequence corrected from an initial overstatement), added the two missing PANOPTICON tests and the a11y linkage, then re-verified everything end to end before this commit.

body:
Closes #100.

`LiveInterviewRecording.session` était en `onDelete: Cascade` : supprimer une session effaçait la preuve en base **en laissant l'objet audio dans R2** — exactement l'audio que la notice de confidentialité candidat, livrée hier, promet « définitivement supprimé ». Correctif conforme à la décision du ticket : un invariant garanti par la base, pas un nouveau workflow. La clé étrangère passe en `Restrict`, et `EraseRecordingsForSession` reste l'unique chemin qui retire de l'audio — objet supprimé **avant** l'écriture du tombstone.

## Le vrai travail : ce que la contrainte casse

Trois chemins suppriment des lignes de session. Deux se seraient mis à échouer en production :

- **La purge Go des previews** supprimait les sessions expirées en une seule instruction. Une seule ligne porteuse d'enregistrement aurait levé une erreur de clé étrangère, annulé toute la transaction — nettoyage des snapshots compris — et **bloqué définitivement** la limitation de conservation pour tous les espaces. Elle contourne désormais ces sessions et les journalise par id.
- **Le nettoyage des previews expirés côté console** tourne *dans la transaction qui crée un preview* : la même erreur aurait fait échouer le bouton du recruteur. Il exclut maintenant les previews bloqués des **deux** suppressions, gardant snapshot et session ensemble pour que la paire reste résolvable.
- **Le reset du smoke** est laissé tel quel volontairement : il découvre déjà les contraintes bloquantes génériquement et nomme la table. Lui apprendre à supprimer des lignes d'enregistrement aurait créé précisément le chemin de suppression non sûr que ce ticket interdit.

## Propriétés épinglées

- Un enregistrement **tombstoné garde sa ligne** : l'effacement seul ne débloque donc jamais une suppression de session (test dédié).
- Un enregistrement **en cours** arrête l'egress et conserve sa ligne jusqu'à ce que la finalisation ou l'effacement aboutisse — comportement déjà correct depuis #162 ; les nouveaux tests le verrouillent plutôt qu'ils ne l'introduisent (rapporté honnêtement par l'implémenteur : verrous de non-régression, pas tests rouges).
- Un échec de suppression R2 laisse `object_key` et le statut intacts pour un réessai.

Corrige au passage un test de #162 qui comparait le statut post-effacement à une valeur locale d'avant l'append : `session_started` fait légitimement passer la ligne en `in_progress`, l'assertion ne tenait que parce que la suite est ignorée sans base de données.

## Vérification

Go contre vrai Postgres : 175 tests, 8 paquets, tous verts (package `store` réellement exécuté) · console 289 tests sur `src/server/interviews` · `pnpm typecheck` et `pnpm test` 19/19 · smoke FR seed **puis reset** Pass (le reset supprime bien la session live du run précédent — le chemin exact que ce changement pouvait casser).

QA : **APPROVE** après mutation testing de chaque assertion porteuse — FK remise en Cascade, ordre d'effacement inversé, statut effacé, garde retirée : chaque test censé attraper la régression l'a attrapée, arbre restauré et revérifié. Balayage indépendant confirmant qu'aucun quatrième chemin de suppression n'existe, et que ni `Organization` ni `CandidateSession` ne cascadent vers les sessions live (pas de relation, seulement une colonne `realtimeSessionId`).

author: harlan-zw
body:
### Description

Runner containers are ephemeral with no shared store, so every job restored the whole dependency set from GitHub's cache service. Measured from this host that service runs at **1.3-4.3 MB/s**, because all the containers share one uplink.

It was slower than not caching at all.

- nuxtseo.com: a **66s** restore replaced a **14s** warm install.
- gscdump.com: five jobs of one run each pulled the **same** 340 MB tarball. 1.79 GB per run, and **417s of an 829s run, half its CI wall time**.
- A run whose cache came back empty reinstalled from npm in **19s**, beating the working-cache path by ~175s.

The store cache also self-poisons: the same key served 410 MB at 08:55 and 6,824 bytes at 09:16, and once a near-empty entry lands under a lockfile hash the post step reports a hit and never re-saves.

Containers now mount one shared content-addressed store, so a job resolves from local disk. The desktop setup action drops `cache: pnpm` to match.

### Verified before shipping, not assumed

- `npm_config_store_dir=/pnpm-store` resolves the store onto the volume (`pnpm store path` -> `/pnpm-store/v10`).
- uid 1001 can write it, and an install populates it.
- The image bakes no Node, npm or pnpm, so the entrypoint needs overriding for the chown step. My first version of `ensure_pnpm_store` got this wrong and failed silently; the committed one passes `--entrypoint chown` and I ran it to confirm.
- After restart, `docker inspect` shows the mount and the env var on every live container.

The volume is created and chowned to the runner uid at startup, because Docker makes a named volume root-owned and a fresh machine would otherwise fail every install.

### Trade-offs

The store sits on a different device from `_work`, so pnpm copies where it would otherwise hardlink. That costs a few seconds against the minute it saves. Recovering hardlinks means moving `_work` onto the same volume, which needs per-container cleanup, so I have not done it.

The store grows without bound and wants pruning on a timer, never during a job. Not in this change.

A GitHub-hosted job has no shared store and should still cache. gscdump's cloud deploy sets that up in its own workflow and is untouched; the desktop action is desktop-only by name and by use.

Consumer side: harlan-zw/nuxtseo.com#346.

The `npm ci` half of #16 — it landed on the branch just after that PR merged, so only the `.gitignore` fix reached `main`.

The first real Vercel deploy failed at exit 127:

```
sh: 1: vite: not found
Error: Command "vite build" exited with 127
```

`vercel build` runs the project's build command, but invoked outside Vercel's own builder it does **not** install dependencies first — so `vite build` ran against an empty `node_modules`. The job's `setup-node` cache restores `~/.npm`, not `node_modules`, so nothing supplied the binary.

Adds `npm ci` before the build, matching what the `web` job already does. Jobs don't share a filesystem, so each needs its own install.

**The secrets were correct** — the CLI authenticated, retrieved the project and downloaded production settings before reaching the build. `Deploy API (Render)` succeeded on the same run, health poll included.

author: vitbokisch
body:
## What

Applies the existing `_d1`/`_d` two-tier idiom to the **tracking**-subscriber channel: the first tracking subscriber lives in an inline `_s1` field, a second promotes to the `_s` Set, and there is no demotion.

A census of the row-list and computed-chain workloads found the tracking-subscriber count is **exactly 1 in 100% of measured cases** (500/500 row-list, 400/400 computed chain), so the Set — and its hashed add/delete — was pure overhead on the dominant shape.

## Measured

Real **Chromium/V8** (never bun — JSC reports `Set.delete` at ~6.7ns vs V8's ~19.3ns, a ~2.9× gap that would flip the verdict on a Set-vs-slot question). Two independent 15-pass runs, **page-isolated per arm**, round-robin with per-pass order rotation, median + bootstrap CI95, timer-clamp guard (every region ≥14× the 100µs quantum). Load **4.25–6.87** throughout, stamped per run. Each arm is a real production bundle of real library code, and the driver re-verifies **from the loaded module** which arm it is running before any sample is taken.

| region | baseline | tier | ratio | CI95 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| dispose 50k tracked effects | 2.500 ms | 1.400 ms | **1.79×** | disjoint (both runs) |
| 50k writes, 20-deep computed chain | 41.6 / 42.5 ms | 35.7 / 35.6 ms | **1.17–1.19×** | disjoint (both runs) |
| 20k batches × 10 writes | 8.9 / 8.8 ms | 7.7 / 8.0 ms | **1.10–1.16×** | disjoint (both runs) |
| 300k writes, 1 tracked subscriber | 7.0 / 7.0 ms | 6.4 / 6.5 ms | **1.08–1.09×** | disjoint (both runs) |
| 20k subscription mounts | 2.0 ms | 1.8 ms | 1.11× | **tie** (overlapped in run 2) |
| 5k writes × 50 subscribers | 8.2 / 8.1 ms | 8.2 / 8.3 ms | **tie** | the Set path — unchanged, as intended |

CV 1.4–12.7%. **Reported as ties: mount and fan-out.** The fan-out row is the regression guard and it is flat, which is the intended outcome — that path still goes through the promoted Set in both arms.

The notify win is a **deleted allocation**, not a micro-tweak: reaching the sole subscriber required `_s.values().next().value`, materialising a Set iterator *plus* an iterator-result object on **every write**. `propagateLazyDirty`'s fused chain walk now hops via the inline slot for the same reason, which is where the 1.17× deep-chain number comes from.

## What this does NOT prove

- **No end-to-end row-list win is claimed, and none should be.** This is a JS-only saving that lands below the resolution floor of the DOM benchmark: `clear rows` is timer-quantised at 100µs — the suite's own verdict line reports it *"too fast to time (<0.1ms)"* — against a subscriber-teardown saving of ~22µs for a 1,000-row clear (22ns × 1,000 removals, measured). A same-window `bench:fair` A/B was attempted with both arms gated by a dist-marker check (tier dist: 17 `_s1` hits, baseline dist: 0), but a load spike to 44 hit the second arm and cross-run medians cannot resolve a 0.22-quantum effect regardless. Discarded rather than reported.
- The micro-benchmark is author-written and author-judged.
- Nothing here is measured on a real app; the regions are synthetic primitive workloads.

## Correctness

`deps` now records the **host** rather than the host's subscriber Set — there is no Set to record while a source has one subscriber. That also makes verify-mode dep reuse strictly *more* stable: the `_suspendSoleSubscriber` container swap used to change `host._s`'s identity and spuriously diverge every effect tracking that signal.

**The store's suspend/resume window is preserved, not weakened.** The token becomes the detached listener in the inline-slot shape and stays the detached Set in the promoted-then-shrunk shape; the caller only ever null-checks it. Verified empirically that the fast path is still *taken*, that a newcomer subscribing mid-window is not clobbered, and that the >1-subscriber shape still falls back to `_suspendSubscriber`. The former "same Set object restored" identity contract is no longer load-bearing, because deps records hosts and `subscribe()` disposers now remove via the host.

### Latent bug fixed along the way

`@pyreon/solid-compat`'s `createStore` sweep tested `_s` alone, so it reported "unused" for the dominant single-subscriber shape and **evicted a live signal**, after which writes to that path stopped re-running its effect. The tier-aware check is now owned by `@pyreon/reactivity` as `_hasSubscribers()` (covering `_s1`/`_s`/`_d1`/`_d`) — exactly the extraction the anti-patterns catalog already prescribes once a second consumer appears.

**Bisect-verified:** reverting `_hasSubscribers` to the Set-only check fails the new solid-compat spec with `expected 2 to be greater than 2` (the effect never re-ran after a leaf write) plus 3 reactivity specs; restored, all pass. Note the pre-existing *"actively-subscribed signals survive the sweep"* spec passes against the bug — it asserts a **parent-path** write, which re-notifies through the parent signal regardless of whether the leaf was evicted. The new spec asserts a **leaf** write, which is the shape that actually discriminates.

Devtools and `debug()` were also updated to walk both tiers; a Set-only count would have reported **zero** subscribers for the overwhelmingly common shape and blanked the reactive graph.

## Suites

reactivity **782** · runtime-dom **1314** · store **215** · core **665** · solid-compat **259** · flow **466** · perf-harness **229** — all green. `validate-fast`: 36/36.

## Unrelated hunk

`docs/src/content/docs/troubleshooting.md` is **pre-existing drift on main** (anti-pattern catalog 274 → 275, generated from a file this PR never touches). `check-generated-fresh` compares the working tree against HEAD, so it has to ride along for the gate to pass.

## Follow-up not taken here

The anti-patterns entry *"Detecting 'has direct subscribers' by reading `signal._d` alone"* still says a helper should be extracted "if a second consumer surfaces". That has now happened and `_hasSubscribers()` exists, so the entry's guidance is stale — worth updating, left out of this PR to keep it to code.

## Reproduce

```
bun /path/to/probe/run.ts            # PROBE_PASSES=15, Chromium, page-isolated per arm
bun run --filter='@pyreon/reactivity' --filter='@pyreon/store' --filter='@pyreon/solid-compat' test
```

💡 What:
Replaced the complex manual string scanning loop in `extractUrls` with a single, precompiled global regular expression (`URL_EXTRACTION_REGEX = /https?:\/\/[^\s"'<>]+/g`).

🎯 Why:
The previous implementation relied heavily on index lookups (`indexOf`), substrings, and nested `while` loops evaluating characters one-by-one via `charCodeAt`. This approach caused excessive overhead and unnecessary allocations for large bodies of text. Outsourcing the heavy lifting to V8's highly optimized native C++ regex engine significantly reduces CPU cycles on the hot path of scanning incoming emails.

📊 Impact:
Microbenchmarks show that replacing the manual string parsing loop with the precompiled global regex speeds up URL token extraction by approximately 25-30% for realistically sized strings, significantly lowering memory overhead and reducing the time the extension blocks when parsing large emails.

🔬 Measurement:
A custom Node.js benchmark script (`benchmark_v8_token_regex.js`) evaluated 50 iterations over a very large text sample (10,000 concatenated strings with mixed URLs). ## This PR contains:

- [x] Changes to dev-tools e.g. CI config / github tooling

### What is the current behavior? (You can also link to an open issue here)

The PR-gate `test` job runs pytest with 4 xdist workers (since #4935). xdist's
default `--dist load` hands each worker a large contiguous slice of the
collection up front, and collection is file-ordered, so cost clusters travel as
a unit — one worker can end up holding several of the expensive integration
files while its peers go idle.

Measured from the `test-report-log.jsonl` artifacts of all five Build runs that
have run with 4 workers so far (10 matrix legs, 13,245–13,250 tests each). Per
leg: each worker's busy time, the leg's average (its ideal per-worker share),
and the resulting imbalance.

| Run | Leg | worker busy times | max | leg avg | imbalance | test-phase wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32229091541 | 3.10 | 161 / **266** / 155 / 163 | 266s | 186s | **+80s** | 271s |
| 32229091541 | 3.11 | 182 / 182 / 181 / 213 | 213s | 189s | +23s | 218s |
| 32229392189 | 3.10 | 153 / **256** / 151 / 156 | 256s | 179s | **+77s** | 261s |

| 32232447154 | 3.11 | 146 / 149 / 145 / **248** | 248s | 172s | **+76s** | 254s |
| 32232453887 | 3.10 | 174 / 155 / **259** / 145 | 259s | 183s | **+76s** | 265s |
| 32232453887 | 3.11 | 184 / 204 / 194 / 188 | 204s | 192s | +12s | 209s |

**4 of 10 legs stranded 76–80s on a single worker.** The straggler in
32229091541/3.10 was one worker holding `test_eval_set.py` (49s) *and*
`test_sample_limits.py` (32s) *and* `test_cancellation_logging.py` (10s), while
the worker that finished 111s earlier had drawn the cheap `agent/deepagent` and
`model` directories.

A Build run waits for the slower of its two matrix legs, so the recoverable wall
clock per run is `max(leg wall) − leg avg`: **81s, 71s, 26s, 62s, 73s** across

### What is the new behavior?

`--dist worksteal` is added to the pytest `addopts` in `pyproject.toml`. It lets
an idle worker take pending tests back off a straggler instead of waiting for it.

15GB, xdist 3.8.0), full suite, same command CI uses. All five runs produced

body:
## Problem

Adding a Firebase source fails schema discovery entirely when the project's default database is provisioned in Datastore mode instead of Native mode, even though Auth users and Realtime Database paths are still readable.

Google's Firestore Documents API (`listCollectionIds`, used to enumerate Firestore collections) only works against Native-mode databases. A Datastore-mode database answers every call with `400 Bad Request` / `FAILED_PRECONDITION`, and that error was not recognized, so it propagated and broke the whole schema listing instead of just excluding Firestore.

Surfaced by an error-tracking issue: `HTTPError: 400 Client Error: Bad Request for url: https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/.../databases/(default)/documents:listCollectionIds`.

## Changes

- `get_tables()` now skips Firestore collections and keeps listing Auth users and Realtime Database paths when the database is in Datastore mode, matching the existing behavior for a missing database (404) or a missing role (403).
- The skip is matched on Google's structured error detail (`FAILED_PRECONDITION` / "Datastore Mode" in the response body), not the bare 400 status code, so an unrelated 400 still surfaces as a real failure.
- `_request()` now appends Google's structured error detail (status and message from the response body) to the raised `HTTPError`, which is what makes that distinction possible. This is mechanical and affects only the exception message text.

## How did you test this code?

Added two test groups to `test_firebase.py`:

- `test_datastore_mode_database_does_not_hide_the_other_tables`: a 400 with a Datastore-mode body still returns Auth users as a table, catching the regression this PR fixes.
- `test_other_firestore_errors_propagate` (parametrized): a 500, and a 400 for an unrelated reason, both still raise — guards against the skip being too broad.

Ran the full `test_firebase.py` suite locally (88 passed).

Not run: mypy (the repo-wide strict run did not finish locally in this session; CI's own mypy job covers it).

None; no user-facing config or workflow changed.

body:
Follow-up to #174. That PR made `/api/health` able to report a commit; production then answered `commitSource: "manus"`, which is the publish stamp rather than a git commit. This closes that gap.

**Conflict resolved.** `scripts/bundle-server.mjs` conflicted because #174 landed as a squash — main carries my earlier inline env chain under a new hash, so git could not see it as the same work. Both sides were mine; the branch's version supersedes main's (the chain moved into `scripts/buildSha.mjs` to be testable), so the merge takes the branch side and the docstring is updated to match. Merged main in rather than rebasing, per the repo's merge-commit convention.

## Where the SHA was being lost

The documented deploy path (`docker compose build`, runbook §3b) builds inside Docker, and all three conditions line up there:

| | |
|---|---|
| `.dockerignore:20` | excludes `.git` |
| `Dockerfile:21` | `COPY . .` — so no history reaches the builder |
| `Dockerfile:24` | `RUN NODE_ENV=production pnpm build` — no CI environment either |

Both sources #174 reads were therefore empty inside the builder, and the runtime fell back to `__manus__/version.json`. Not a dashboard setting — a repo one.

## Changes

- **`Dockerfile`** — builder stage takes `ARG GIT_COMMIT_SHA` and exports it, feeding `VITE_BUILD_SHA` from the same value so the client bundle and `/api/health` can never name different commits.
- **`docker-compose.yml`** — forwards `GIT_COMMIT_SHA` from the environment as a build arg.
- **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`** — the image-build job passes `github.sha`, so the CI image is identifiable too.
- **`docs/DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md`** — §3b now reads `GIT_COMMIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD) docker compose build`, and §5a gains a `commitSource` table for post-deploy verification.
- **`docs/MANUS_BUILD_COMMIT_SHA.md`** — the operator instruction for a Manus build that runs outside our Dockerfile: build command, `docker build --build-arg`, or dashboard variable. It calls out that the variable must be scoped to the **build** step, not runtime — the usual mistake, and one that would look identical to the current symptom.
- **`scripts/audits/run-stale-document-codes.mjs`** — read-only runner for the audit script from #174 (see note below).

## Two supporting fixes

**The env chain masked itself.** It was first-*defined*, not first-*non-empty*. The Docker builder sets `GIT_COMMIT_SHA` unconditionally from the ARG, so `??` stopped on the empty string and never reached `GITHUB_SHA` — which would have silently broken the CI image build too. The selection rule moved to `scripts/buildSha.mjs` so it is testable without running esbuild; 9 tests cover precedence, the empty and whitespace cases, and trimming.

**A build with no SHA now says so.** It used to produce an untraceable artifact quietly, which is how this survived three deploys:

```
[bundle-server] No commit SHA available — /api/health will fall back to the published
version stamp. Set one of GIT_COMMIT_SHA, … at build time (see docs/DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md §3b).
```

## Verified

Against all three configurations a build can be in, by staging a `.git`-less copy to reproduce the Docker builder:

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| no `.git`, no env — *today's production* | warns, bakes nothing → falls back to the version stamp |
| `GIT_COMMIT_SHA` supplied — *what the ARG does* | bakes `abc123def456` |
| empty `GIT_COMMIT_SHA` + `GITHUB_SHA` — *the masking bug* | correctly falls through to `fedcba987654` |

A normal local build on the merge commit bakes `b3b1b7af05cf`, matching `git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD`.

Full suite **9,162 passed / 4 skipped** on the merged tree, `pnpm check` clean, both YAML files parse, zero migrations.

## Note on the stale-code audit

The publish checkpoint on main records the audit as **empty across all four queries** — production holds no legacy-coded `document_types` rows and no filings under one. So there is no re-filing list, and TEST-CHECKLIST-2 was the local reproduction rather than a stale-code casualty. The runner is included anyway so the check is repeatable rather than a one-off.

## After the next deploy

```sh
curl -s https://<host>/api/health | jq '{commit, commitSource, builtAt}'
```

`commitSource: "build"` means it worked. Still `"manus"` means Manus builds outside our Dockerfile — `docs/MANUS_BUILD_COMMIT_SHA.md` is the instruction to hand whoever owns that pipeline.

body:
`grep -rn "permission_role" lib/**/*.ex 2>/dev/null | head -6` opened a confirmation dialog and stopped the run:

```
danger-guard: waiting for the user to approve writes over outside the workspace: /dev/null
```

The redirect target was resolved as a path like any other, landed outside the session root, and hit the "writes over outside the workspace" rule meant for real files. `2>/dev/null` is about the most ordinary command shape there is, and a dialog on it is pure prompt-fatigue — the thing the tiering is designed to avoid spending.

A redirect to the bit bucket writes *through*, not *over*. Redirect targets matching `DEV_SINK` — `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/full`, `/dev/tty`, `/dev/std{in,out,err}`, `/dev/fd/N`, `/dev/u?random` — are skipped before the path tier.

Exact match, deliberately not `/dev/*`:

- `cat disk.img > /dev/sda` is still **block** (that's a separate regex rule on block devices, untouched).
- `rm -rf /dev/null` is a delete, not a redirect, so it still goes through the normal path tier — **confirm**.
- `echo x > /dev/nullish` is a file in `/dev` and still **confirm**.

Those three are now pinned by tests, along with five allow cases. `make test` — 131 pass, 0 fail.

Note: this branches off `main` and is independent of #9, but both touch the redirect loop in `pathVerdicts`, so whichever lands second will want a trivial rebase.

body:
## Description

In the chat area, images in an **agent's markdown reply** that use a relative path (e.g. `![](./chart.png)`) fail to render, while user-uploaded images (absolute paths) render fine. Both hit `POST /api/fs/image-base64`; the failing request has payload `{"path":"./material.jpeg"}` with no `workspace`, and the backend returns 400.

Root cause is a missing wiring in `AcpChat` (the chat surface for external ACP agents like Claude Code):

- `LocalImageView` resolves image paths against a `root` taken from context (default `''`). The only place that sets a non-empty `root` was `AionrsChat` (via `LocalImageView.Provider` + `updateLocalImage({ root: workspace })`). `AcpChat` receives the same `workspace` prop but never fed it into that context.
- With `root=''`, `LocalImageView` short-circuits and posts the bare relative path with `workspace: undefined`. The backend `validate_path` then `canonicalize`s the relative path against **aioncore's own process cwd** (not the agent cwd), fails, and returns `BadRequest` → 400.

Fix (frontend-only, mirrors `AionrsChat`): wrap `AcpChat` in `LocalImageView.Provider` and set `root = workspace`. Relative paths then join the agent cwd, and `workspace` is also sent as the fs sandbox root (the backend appends it to the allowed roots, so agent project dirs pass validation). No backend change is required.

author: ashnar2602
body:
Three small, independent bug fixes found while working with this codebase:

1. **`XGDException::what()` always returned an empty string.** `full_message_`, the field backing `what()`, was declared in `XGDException.h` but never assigned anywhere. `log_error()` built the real error text into a local variable and only ever sent it to `std::cerr`, so any `catch (const XGDException& e)` block that logs `e.what()` got nothing useful. Fixed by assigning `full_message_` in `log_error()`.

2. **`XGDLog`'s destructor bypassed the configured output sink.** The destructor wrote straight to `std::cerr` instead of going through the same path as an explicit `<< Endl`. Several call sites (e.g. the catch blocks in `InputHelper.cpp`) build a line ending in `\n` and rely on the destructor to flush it, so those lines never reached whatever `Endl` is actually wired to (e.g. the GUI's log view). Fixed by routing the destructor through `operator<<(Endl)`.

3. **No timeouts on `TitleHelper`'s curl requests.** `internet_connected()`, `set_ogx_titles_online()`, `unity_query()`, and `unity_get_title_icon()` all call `curl_easy_perform()` without `CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT`/`CURLOPT_TIMEOUT`. On a slow or unreachable network this can hang indefinitely with no feedback. Added reasonable timeouts to all four.

Each fix is its own commit. No functional/behavioral changes beyond what's described above.

author: arcz
body:
The Upsample 9-to-8 adapter contains a use-after-free: it passes an initializer-owned name by reference to `Graph::eraseInitializer`, which destroys the string before subsequent bookkeeping reuses it. Copy the name before erasure and add regression coverage using a heap-backed initializer name.

Reproducer: [model.onnx.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31218118/model.onnx.zip)

The reproducer contains an opset-9 Upsample node with initializer-backed scales and triggers the use-after-free when converted to opset 8.

```python
import onnx

model = onnx.load("model.onnx")
onnx.checker.check_model(model)
onnx.version_converter.convert_version(model, 8)
```

### Security Impact
A checker-accepted ONNX model can trigger this use-after-free during explicit conversion from opset 9 to 8, potentially crashing the process and causing denial of service. Exploitability appears low because the dangling reference is only read immediately after the free, with no intervening allocation that could replace its model-controlled contents; we found no write primitive, data disclosure, or path to code execution.

### Motivation and Context
This bug was found by Artur Cygan of Trail of Bits in collaboration with OpenAI (Patch the Planet initiative).

body:
Addresses the duplicate-accounts half of #682.

## Problem
A user had **dozens of duplicate "M-Pesa Tanzania" accounts** (last-4s `7926, 3581, 6690, 188, …`, screenshot in the issue). Root cause: mobile-money wallet parsers don't override `extractAccountLast4`, so the base generic regex grabs whatever number is in each SMS — the **counterparty's phone number** (`… to CATHERINE MINJA - Airtel Money (255694XXXXXX)`) or the **"card ending 1915"** — which **varies every transaction**. A mobile wallet has no stable account number, so each transaction minted a new `(bank, last4)` account.

## Fix
Override `extractAccountLast4` to return `null` on the mobile-money **wallet** parsers, so all activity consolidates into one wallet account:
- `MPesaTanzaniaParser`, `SelcomPesaParser`, `MixxByYasParser`, `TigoPesaParser` (the reported TZ family)
- `MPESAParser` (M-Pesa Kenya) — same latent bug (also a stable-account-less wallet)

**Untouched:** real bank parsers (`NMBTanzaniaParser`, `CrdbBankParser`, `DiamondTrustBankParser`) keep their genuine account numbers. Card-payment flagging (`isFromCard`) is unaffected.

## Tests
`TanzaniaParserTest` — added a `@TestFactory` with 16 `assertNull(accountLast4)` checks across received/sent/paid/withdraw/bill shapes for all four TZ wallets, and fixed the two Selcom cases that expected a card last-4. Regenerated `bank-samples.json` (the `BankSamplesDocTest` sync gate). Full `./init.sh parser` green (independently re-run).

## Out of scope (deliberately)
- **Prevention only** — this stops *new* duplicates; a user's *existing* duplicates need a separate consolidation/merge (not built here).
- The `[OR-FGEMF-20]` subscription decline in the same issue is a **Google Play** billing decline, not app code.

Duas extrações para `ui/pure.js` e uma limpeza que estava pendente desde o passo 2.

Decide entre quatro estados: sem conta, token inválido, erro na última checagem, ou silêncio. Saiu com `if` planos em vez de ternário encadeado **por medida**: a escada subiria o `pure.js` de `ternarioAninhado: 16` para `17`, e esse arquivo tem folga **zero** nesse eixo.

Confirma o que o app fez ("aprovou 3 PRs sozinho hoje") em vez de só dizer que não tem nada. Singular/plural de PR e de minuto passam a ser testáveis.

Símbolos importados do `pure.js` que ninguém mais usava, acumulados pelos passos 2 a 5 — todos meus. **Import morto não quebra nada e por isso apodrece:** passa por `node --check`, pelo lint, pela suíte inteira e pelo CI. O `ui/app.js` foi de 101 para 84 símbolos importados (86 depois das duas extrações novas).

Agora tem guarda em `test/app-carrega.test.js`. Provado por mutação: reintroduzi um import não usado, o teste falhou; removi, voltou ao verde.

Não é a suíte verde — é prova diferencial. Para cada extração, reconstruí o bloco antigo a partir de `git show HEAD:ui/app.js` com o DOM neutralizado e comparei string contra string numa matriz de entradas:

body:
> **Based on `feat/german-element-defaults` (#91), not `main`** — it needs the
> German tables. Merge #91 first and this retargets cleanly.

Modelled on the introduction dialog in simple-todo's `qr01`, split where the seam
actually is.

## Two halves

**The story is the app's**, through the default slot — what this app is for, who
the other person is, what a passkey means here. None of that belongs in a
transport.

**The caveats are the library's**: whether a phone holds a waiting invite,
whether Chrome on Android reports IPv6, what carrier NAT does, what a VPN does.
Those are the top facts in this project's own `AGENTS.md`. Every consumer needs
them and today each writes them again from memory.

Between them sits a live verdict, because advice is only worth giving when it
applies. `sameNetwork` sits *next to* the verdict rather than folded into it:
telling two phones already sharing a Wi-Fi to find another network would be wrong.

## The one thing I did differently from qr01

**It reuses `probeNetwork`.** qr01 wrote a second, smaller probe for its
introduction — candidate found yes or no, no address family, no notion of a
symmetric NAT — and said why:

> *This runs its own gathering rather than reusing `qr-status`, because that
> element renders only in the technical view.*

That is a layout problem being solved twice at the wrong layer, and the thin
verdict lands on the reader least equipped to interpret one. `renderResult` and
`probeNetwork` already exist for exactly this.

## The policy is separate, and DOM-free

An app writing its own introduction still wants the rule, and the rule is the
part that is easy to get wrong. Three decisions, each of which one would make the
other way on a first attempt:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| arriving by invite suppresses it | that person came to accept something — and suppressing does **not** mark it seen, so they get it next visit |
| blocked storage shows it | seen twice beats never seen |
| `forget()` exists | dismissing must not be a one-way door |

## Two real findings from the specs

**`dialog.close()` fires no `close` event in the Chromium these specs run on.**
Depending on it loses the event; listening on both paths without a guard sends it
twice. The element keeps its own `#open` flag and emits from whichever path ran
first. I saw this once before in the demo and wrote it off as an automation
artifact — it is not, and that earlier conclusion was wrong.

**`shadowRoot.textContent` proves nothing about what is visible** — it includes
the stylesheet and every hidden node. My first spec asserted on it and failed
against its own style block. The specs now use Playwright locators, which pierce
an open shadow root *and* respect `hidden`.

## Also here

The German drift guard grew an **array** comparison. The intro's caveat list is
four sentences — the longest prose in any of these tables — and the previous
check only inspected strings, so leaving that list in English would have passed.
Proven by counter-test: reverting one sentence to English turns it red.

## Verified

105 package tests, 112 chromium and 106 firefox specs, both locales build.

## What ships

**Builds now fail when a deployment's env is incomplete.** Every `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is inlined at build time, and the defaults for the four deployment-specific vars are *localhost* values — so a box missing one silently baked a broken URL into its bundle and deployed green. That is the shape of both `fix/public-env-static-inline` and `fix/websocket-url-static-inline`.

- `src/config/env.ts` throws for `API_URL` / `APP_URL` / `APP_ENV` / `STORAGE_URL`, during a production build or SSR only — never in the browser, where the value is already inlined and throwing could only white-screen a working app.
- `.env.example` added (this repo has never had one, while `src/` uses **18** distinct `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` vars).
- `scripts/check-env.mjs` wired as `prebuild`, so it gates every `npm run build` with **no deploy script on any box needing an edit**.
- CI builds against `.env.example`, proving the documented contract is sufficient.
- Dependabot: weekly, grouped.

Also carries the CI improvements already on `development` — unit tests with a zero-test guard, base-branch-aware conflict check, and the deploy retry backoff.

## Verified on staging

Both staging deploys ran the gate for real:

```
> node scripts/check-env.mjs
env check: 18 documented, 4 required vars present.
✓ Compiled successfully in 119s
```

`staging-app.lendyph.com` and `binhs-coop-staging.lendyph.com` both at `930346b`, HTTP 307 (the `/` → `/login` redirect), pm2 online.

All five frontends were checked beforehand and **have all four required vars**, so no production build can be blocked by this change. If one were missing, the deploy would now fail loudly instead of shipping a bundle pointed at localhost — which is the entire point.

body:
## Summary

Fixes a bug where `tasks report --by-tag --from <date> --to <date>` always showed `Pending=0` and `Completion%=100.0%` because only completed tasks were considered when a date range was active.

## Root Cause

In `_build_tag_report`, the date-range branch filtered tasks by `completed_at`, which is `None` for all pending tasks. This meant pending tasks were always excluded, making `pending` always `0` and `Completion %` always `100.0%`.

## Fix

Introduced a helper `_task_in_date_range(task, from_dt, to_dt)` that applies the correct date field depending on task state:

- **Completed tasks** → filtered by `completed_at`
- **Pending tasks** → filtered by `created_at`

`_build_tag_report` now uses this helper uniformly, so pending tasks created within the date range are included in the aggregation alongside completed tasks whose completion date falls in range.

## Behaviour Change

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Pending task created in range | excluded | included |
| Pending count | always `0` in date-range mode | correct non-zero value |
| Completion % | always `100.0%` in date-range mode | accurate percentage |
| No date range | unchanged | unchanged |

## Tests Added

- Unit tests for `_task_in_date_range` covering all branches (pending/completed, in/out of range, boundary dates, missing dates).
- Unit tests for `_build_tag_report` verifying correct totals, pending counts, and completion percentages.
- CLI integration tests using `typer.testing.CliRunner` verifying end-to-end report output for mixed, all-pending, and out-of-range scenarios.

Six screenshots and the demo GIF, all captured by driving a real headless Chrome over CDP against `wrangler dev` — the same runtime Cloudflare runs, so this is the deployed build rather than a dev server. No MCP server was involved; Node 22's built-in WebSocket speaks CDP directly. No screen recording, so nothing is staged.

## The GIF

Two sessions do the same thing: build a submit-ready draft through the mock's own API, walk to the wizard's review step, click **Submit for distribution**. The only difference is `?cache=naive`.

- **events mode** — the release is the first row on the board you land on, `10 in pipeline`
- **naive cache** — the same board, `9 in pipeline`, no release

Frames carry their elapsed time since the click, so the two sides are paired on when things happened rather than on frame number. 9 seconds, 8fps, 1522×622, 370KB.

Two decisions that determine whether it reads at all:

- **Sidebars cropped.** The same nav rendered twice costs the tables the pixels they need; without the crop the row titles are unreadable at README width.
- **The release is "Ion Weather", not "Signal Fade".** The test helper's title is already a seeded release, so the first cut showed two Signal Fades on the left and asked the viewer to compare catalogue numbers to find the point.

It also confirms, in a browser rather than in prose, what ADR-002's sharp-edges note says: do not try to film an appear-then-vanish flicker. Naive mode never shows the release at all.

## The screenshots

| Shot | Why this one |
|---|---|
| catalog | Filtered to live releases: the default newest-first page is drafts, whose Trend and Streams columns are empty by definition. Doubles as proof that filters are URL state. |
| distribution | Timeline strip, store progress (`0/5`, `2/5`, `4/5`), and the mix of pipeline states. |
| wizard-review | Three blocking issues, each with its own action, and Submit disabled behind them. |
| analytics | The 90-day window, where the seeded playlist surge is visible; tooltip on the peak (1,222,030, +10.1%). 30d is a flat line. |
| activity | The event vocabulary on screen: `domain/releases/submitted`, `domain/tracks/processed`. |
| release-detail | LOR-0042, eleven tracks with ISRCs, 5/5 delivered with timestamps. |

Each carries the architectural claim it demonstrates rather than a decorative caption. Downscaled to 1440 wide — the README renders them near 900, and the 2× originals cost three times the bytes for nothing visible. 1.6MB for six stills plus the GIF.

Every image was inspected before it went in, which caught a broken one: `/catalog/neon-arterial` rendered "This release could not be loaded", because release ids are catalogue numbers (`lor-0042`), not title slugs. Every image link in the README resolves.

## What
- Variant builder: the custom-redemption checkbox is now "השתמש בטקסט מימוש ותקנון מותאמים לוריאנט זה" and reveals terms + method + an https-only tkanon field (seeded from the offer-level link). `draftToPayload` normalizes vs the shared values: a seeded field left unchanged stays INHERITED live - override only tkanon and the terms/method keep following the offer.
- Shared-variant manual form/import carry tkanon as a template; `diffSharedLinkedFields` dropped terms/method - write-through to the shared record is face/stackable/sku/tags only (per-offer text/link edits never touch other adopters).
- Benefits Partnerships: the main-table tkanon column moved INSIDE the per-variant expander (`VariantDetailsTable` shows each variant's effective link with the reused `bpcRegulations` tooltip; expander colSpan 14 -> 13).

## Verification
- tsc -b + vite build green. Lint fails only on pre-existing `GroupSelect.tsx` errors already on development.
- Owner manual pass done.

Pairs with nexus-website PR #246 (backend first) + the nexusWallet PR.
